description:
`@MicroserviceTest` is a JUnit 5 extension that boots a **whole `Microservice`** — config, lifecycle, and an embedded Jetty server on an ephemeral port — for the duration of a test class, then stops it cleanly. It's the standalone-microservice analog of Spring's `@SpringBootTest`, and it composes the existing [`@TestBean` mock-bean substrate](/docs/topics/RestServerTestBeanInjection) for collaborator substitution.

It ships in a small dedicated support module:

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId>
    <artifactId>juneau-microservice-test</artifactId>
    <version>${juneau.version}</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

## When to use it (vs. `MockRestClient`)

The two integration-test paths are intentionally distinct:

| Use | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`@MicroserviceTest`** | A genuine full-microservice test — real server, real connectors, real lifecycle, exercised over HTTP. |
| **`MockRestClient`** | An in-JVM test of a single `@Rest` resource — no server, no sockets, dispatched directly against a `RestContext`. |

`MockRestClient` does **not** talk to a booted server; reach for `@MicroserviceTest` when you want the actual server, filters, and connector path in the loop.

## Specifying the system under test

The SUT is declared **explicitly** (no classpath scanning), two complementary ways:

1. **`configurations={...}`** — one or more `@Configuration` classes whose `@Bean Servlet` methods the microservice auto-mounts (the common case).
2. **A `static Microservice.Builder` supplier method** on the test class (default name `microserviceBuilder`, override via `builderMethod`) — for full control of the builder. Any `configurations={...}` are appended to whatever the supplier returns.

Either way the extension additionally installs an ephemeral-Jetty `Server` (bound to port 0) and `JettyConfiguration`, so tests only contribute their resources. The extension currently boots Jetty.

```java
@MicroserviceTest(configurations = MyServi...

## Contents/Features

Juneau Microservice Jetty is an API for creating stand-alone executable jars that can be used to start lightweight
configurable REST interfaces with all the power of the Juneau REST server and client APIs.

## Zero-config facade

`JettyMicroservice` is a **thin static-call facade** that collapses the standard `Microservice` +
`JettyConfiguration` bootstrap into a single line. For what changed from earlier releases, see the
[v10.0 Migration Guide](/docs/topics/V10MigrationGuide).

### Canonical entry point

```java
public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    JettyMicroservice.run(args, new RootResources()).join();
}
```

That one call boots Jetty on port `10000` (the bundled default), registers your root servlet, starts the interactive
console, and blocks until the process is stopped.

### Three overloads

| Method | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `JettyMicroservice.run(args, rootServlet)` | Starts with the interactive console **enabled** (equivalent to `startConsole=true`). |
| `JettyMicroservice.run(args, rootServlet, startConsole)` | Explicit console opt-in/opt-out. Pass `false` to suppress the interactive prompt. |
| `JettyMicroservice.run(args, beanStore, startConsole, configurations...)` | Power-user form: supply your own `WritableBeanStore` and configuration class list. Use when you need multiple `@Bean Servlet` contributions, custom `MicroserviceListener`s, or a parent bean store. |

All three return the **started** `Microservice` instance; callers wanting "start and block forever" should chain
`.join()` on the result.

### Bundled classpath defaults

The facade's two-argument form pre-wires `JettyConfiguration`, which provides:

- **Port `10000`** — surfaced as `Jetty/port` in the bundled `juneau.cfg`.
- **`jetty.xml`** — a minimal Jetty wiring file. A consumer-supplied copy on the working directory or classpath wins
  via...

description:
> **See also:** [Health / Readiness / Liveness Probes](/docs/topics/HealthProbes) — the probe surface (`/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/livez`) this page gates during shutdown.

Starting with **10.0.0**, both embedded-server microservice flavors — `juneau-microservice-jetty` and `juneau-microservice-tomcat` — perform a **zero-downtime graceful shutdown** suitable for rolling Kubernetes deployments. The two servers share one identical shutdown contract.

When a microservice begins shutting down it:

1. **Flips readiness out of service first.** A shared `ReadinessState` flag is flipped before the listening connector stops, so `GET /readyz` immediately returns `503 Service Unavailable` (`state=OUT_OF_SERVICE`) while a load balancer / Kubernetes is still routing. `GET /livez` and `GET /healthz` stay healthy so the orchestrator does **not** kill the pod mid-drain.
2. **Optionally settles.** An optional `shutdownSettleDelay` pause between the readiness flip and the connector stop gives the load balancer a window to observe the `503` before draining begins.
3. **Drains in-flight requests.** The connector stops accepting new connections and the server waits up to a bounded `stopTimeout` (default `30s`) for in-flight requests to complete before it fully stops.

This sequencing is what lets Kubernetes shift traffic away from a terminating pod before its in-flight work is interrupted.

## Shutdown sequence

```
shutdown begins
   │
   ├─▶ ReadinessState.markOutOfService()      /readyz → 503 (OUT_OF_SERVICE)
   │                                          /livez  → 200  (still LIVE)
   │                                          /healthz→ 200  (still UP)
   │
   ├─▶ sleep(shutdownSettleDelay)             LB observes the 503 (default 0ms)
   │
   ├─▶ drain in-flight requests               up to stopTimeout (default 30s)
   │     Jetty:  server.setStopTimeout(...) then server.stop()
   │     Tomcat: connector.pause() then wait for active count → 0, then stop()
   │
   └─▶ server fully st...

Starting with **10.0.0**, Juneau ships a coherent, discoverable **Actuator-style management surface** while preserving Juneau's a-la-carte composability. Every endpoint exists in two independently-mountable flavors — a composable `*Mixin` and a routed `*Resource` — sharing one worker, and a convenience `BasicActuatorGroup` assembles them under a single configurable path prefix.

## Endpoint catalog

| Endpoint | What it does | Module | Default exposure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /info` | Application manifest / build / version / git metadata | `juneau-microservice` | **on** |
| `GET /loggers`, `GET /loggers/{name}` | Read logger levels (JUL default; Logback/Log4j2 opt-in) | `juneau-rest-server` | **on** |
| `PUT`/`POST /loggers/{name}` | Set a logger level at runtime | `juneau-rest-server` | **deny-by-default** |
| `GET /metrics` | Prometheus scrape from a Micrometer registry | `juneau-rest-server-metrics-micrometer` | on (501 if no registry) |
| `GET /healthz`, `/readyz`, `/livez` | Health / readiness / liveness probes | `juneau-rest-server` | **on** |
| `GET /threaddump` | `ThreadMXBean` thread dump | `juneau-rest-server` | **deny-by-default** |
| `GET /heapdump` | HotSpot `.hprof` heap dump | `juneau-rest-server` | **deny-by-default** |

Endpoints are split across modules by dependency: `/loggers` (JUL backend) and the JDK-only `/threaddump`/`/heapdump` need only the REST server; non-JUL `/loggers` backends (Logback/Log4j2) need `juneau-rest-server-management-logging`; `/metrics` needs Micrometer; `/info` needs the microservice runtime that resolves the application `ManifestFile`.

description:
The `juneau-sc` group provides a **Git-backed configuration server** that exposes
[juneau-config](/docs/topics/JuneauConfig) files stored in a remote Git repository over REST, enabling
centralised configuration management across a fleet of microservices.

| Module | Role |
|--------|------|
| [juneau-sc-server](/docs/topics/ScServerOverview) | A standalone Juneau/Jetty microservice that clones a remote Git repo and serves `.cfg` files as JSON over a REST API. |

## Architecture

```
  Git Remote Repository
  (e.g. GitHub / GitLab)
         │
         │  clone / pull
         ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │       juneau-sc-server      │
  │                             │
  │  GET /configs/{proj}/{br}   │
  │  → JSON (APPLICATION +      │
  │    PROJECT config items)    │
  └────────────┬────────────────┘
               │  HTTP GET
               ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │  Consuming microservice     │
  │  (manual REST call via      │
  │   juneau-rest-client)       │
  └─────────────────────────────┘
```

## Motivation

Juneau's file-based `Config` API is powerful for single-service deployments, but managing dozens of config
files across many pods or VMs becomes error-prone. `juneau-sc` solves this by:

1. **Centralising storage** — a single Git repository holds the canonical copy of every config file.
2. **Version-controlled config** — all changes are tracked with full Git history and branch support.
3. **Layered defaults** — an `application.cfg` file provides shared defaults; each project's `.cfg` file
   supplies project-specific overrides. Both are returned together in a single request.

## Config Repository Layout

The Git repository served by `juneau-sc-server` is expected to follow this flat structure:

```text
<git-repo-root>/
    application.cfg      ← shared defaults (key APPLICATION in the response)
    my-project.cfg       ← project-specific overrides (key PROJECT in the response)
    other-project.cfg
    ...
```

description:
The **juneau-petstore** family is the canonical Apache Juneau showcase application. It packages a small, complete
sample petstore (pets, orders, users) and deploys it under two runtimes, Jetty/`Microservice` and Spring Boot, using
the *exact same* REST surface. Its centrepiece is an admin console built entirely on the Juneau console framework:
fourteen pages that exercise datatables, charts, staged edits, async jobs, themes and the four rendering flavors.
This section tours that console, page by page.

> **In-tree, no external repo.** The petstore lives directly in the Juneau reactor under `juneau-petstore/`.

## Module layout

```
juneau-petstore/                         (top-level aggregator, packaging=pom)
├── juneau-petstore-core/                Shared, deployment-agnostic surface (REST API, console, tests)
├── juneau-petstore-jetty/               Jetty/Microservice deployment
└── juneau-petstore-springboot/          Spring Boot deployment
```

Each module ships as a plain `jar` (no OSGi-bundle wrapping for the sample). The library Juneau modules they depend on
are still OSGi bundles, so OSGi consumers lose nothing.

## What is mounted where

The core-hosted surface is identical across both deployments by construction (it is shared code, not parallel
copies):

| URL | Resource | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `/petstore/*` | `PetStoreResource` | The petstore REST API: `GET`/`POST`/`PUT`/`DELETE` over pets, orders and users, backed by an in-memory `PetStore` service seeded from classpath JSON. |
| `/console/*` | `PetstoreConsoleResource` | The admin console. Each page is a child resource (`StoreRest`, `PetsRest`, `OrdersRest`, `UsersRest`, `OpsRest`, `DevRest`, `AboutRest`) that extends `PetstoreConsolePage`. |
| `/juneau-console/*` | `ConsoleAssetsRest` | The console shell scripts and stylesheets, served by `ConsoleChromeMixin`. |
| `/petstore-ui` | `PetstoreUiResource` | A no-build React app that talks to `/petstore`; the console embeds it as the React renderi...

description:
Every petstore console page shares one chrome: the header with the brand and theme toggle, the navigation tree, the
pending-changes badge and the footer. That chrome is defined once, in the shared `base.ftlh` template, and every
page template wraps itself in it. This page walks the chrome, the navigation tree and the contract test that pins
the pages. For the directives themselves, see [Admin-Console Chrome](/docs/topics/AdminConsoleChrome).

## The base template

Each page's template calls `<@page>`, which captures the page's cards and includes `base.ftlh`. The base template
holds the `<@console>` directive, so the chrome is declared exactly once.

Source: `juneau-petstore-core/src/main/resources/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/templates/base.ftlh`.

```html
<@console brand="Juneau Petstore" title=(pageTitle!"") theme=(petstoreTheme!"open") schemeToggle=true>
<@scripts phase="after-toolkit"><script src="${assetUrl('/console/petstore.js')}"></script></@scripts>
<@navigation>
  <@node id="store" label="Store" href="/console/store"/>
  <@node id="pets" label="Pets" href="/console/pets">
    <@node id="sold" label="Sold" href="/console/pets/sold"/>
    <@node id="changes" label="Pending changes" href="/console/pets/changes"/>
  </@node>
  ...
</@navigation>
<@badge id="pending" src="/console/pets/changes/pending" href="/console/pets/changes" ... placement="header"/>
<@main/>
<@footer text="Apache Juneau petstore sample"/>
</@console>
```

Three things to notice:

- The theme comes from the model (`petstoreTheme`), so the [Themes](/docs/topics/PetstoreThemes) page can switch it.
  A custom theme layers `<@token>` overrides inside a nameless `<@theme>` in the same template.
- `petstore.js` is the one petstore-specific script, loaded after the toolkit on every page.
- The `<@badge>` sits after `</@navigation>` and is unscoped on purpose; see
  [Pending Changes](/docs/topics/PetstorePendingChanges).

description:
The Pets page, served at `/console/pets`, is the petstore's main table. It lists every pet with server-side
searching, sorting and paging, a ribbon of filters, row actions, multi-row selection with a bulk "Mark sold"
action, and export. It is the best single page to read if you want to see what a server-mode
[Rich Table View](/docs/topics/RichTableViews) looks like in a real app.

## What this page shows

![The pets page: a server-mode table with paging, search, per-column filters and row actions](/topics/PetstorePets.Page.1.png)

- **Server mode.** The table posts a DataTables request to `/console/pets/query`. `PetsRest.query` runs it against
  the pet collection with `DataTablesQuery.run`, so searching and ordering are BeanQuery expressions evaluated on
  the server. A malformed search expression comes back as a 200 response carrying an `error` envelope, so the table
  can show the message instead of failing.
- **Ribbon.** Two option groups ("Pet status" with Available and Pending, and "Species" with Mammals and Others)
  that set column filters, an "+ Add pet" dialog button, copy and CSV export (Excel and PDF when available) and
  a refresh button.
- **Row actions.** Edit (a dialog form, merges the row on success) and Delete (with a confirmation).
- **Selection and bulk.** Rows can be selected across pages, except sold pets, which carry the reason "Already
  sold." The bulk action "Mark sold" calls `POST /console/pets/{id}/sell` once per selected row.
- **URL state.** The `ids` URL-state directive carries a comma-separated list of pet ids in the page URL. The query
  endpoint accepts it as `?ids=` and narrows the rows to those ids before the column filters apply.
- **Polling.** The table refreshes every 30 seconds and pauses while a cell is being edited.

The template is `pets.ftlh`. The excerpt keeps the data mode, the URL state and the bulk definition.

description:
The Sold pets page, served at `/console/pets/sold`, is the smallest table page in the petstore: every pet that has
been marked sold, with a species filter. It exists to show the contrast with the main [Pets](/docs/topics/PetstorePets)
page. Same bean, but a different data mode and a much shorter template.

## What this page shows

- A table in **client mode**. The endpoint returns all the rows in one response and the browser does the filtering,
  sorting and paging. There is no server-side query, so the endpoint is a plain `GET` returning a list.
- A ribbon option group that filters on the `species` column in the browser, with no request to the server.
- A **minimal page template**: no tab attribute, no URL state, no row actions.

Client mode is the right choice when the full row set is small. When it is not, use server mode, as the Pets page
does.

## Template

The template is `pets-sold.ftlh`. The card body is trimmed here to its essentials.

```
<@page toolkit="views">
<@card type="datatables" id="sold" title="Sold pets">
{
  rowType: 'Pet',
  dataMode: 'client',
  dataUrl: '/console/pets/sold/rows',
  columns: [ { key: 'id', label: 'Id' }, { key: 'name', label: 'Name' }, { key: 'species', label: 'Species' } ],
  ribbon: [
    { type: 'optionGroup', id: 'species', title: 'Species', options: [
      { id: 'dogs', title: 'Dogs', column: 'species', value: '$eq(DOG)' },
      { id: 'cats', title: 'Cats', column: 'species', value: '$eq(CAT)' } ] },
    { type: 'refresh' } ]
}
</@card>
</@page>
```

The filter values use the BeanQuery search syntax (`$eq(DOG)`). In client mode the table applies them locally; in server
mode the same strings are sent to the server.

The pet detail page is where a console page gets a nested identity. One pet has four tabs (Summary, Photo, Orders and
History) and each tab is its own URL under `/console/pets/{id}/{tab}`. The Orders tab goes one level deeper:
`/console/pets/{id}/orders/{orderId}` selects one of the pet's orders. The navigation tree grows to match, so this
is also the petstore's example of **depth-4 navigation** with nodes that are added per request.

## What this page shows

![The summary tab of pet 1, with its Summary, Photo, Orders and History subtabs](/topics/PetstorePetDetail.Page.1.png)

- **Per-request navigation nodes.** The page appends nodes under the `pets` node: `p<petId>` with children
  `summary`, `photo`, `orders` and `history`, and `o<orderId>` under `orders` when an order is selected. Node ids
  must start with a letter, so the numeric ids are prefixed. The active tab is `pets/p<id>/<tab>`, or
  `pets/p<id>/orders/o<orderId>` at depth 4.

- **Photo** is an `html` card holding an `<object>` that points at the API's own photo endpoint, with fallback text
  when no photo is uploaded. Admins also get an "Upload photo" card; for other viewers the template leaves it out on
  the server.
- **Orders** is a table of this pet's orders with a row detail, plus an `html` card for the selected order.
- **History** is the pet's audit entries, newest first.
- **Not found.** An unknown pet renders `pet-not-found.ftlh` inside the chrome with a 404 status, rather than an
  error page. An unknown tab, or an order that does not exist or belongs to another pet, is a plain 404.

The bare URL `/console/pets/{id}` answers with a 303 to the Summary tab.

description:
The Orders page, served at `/console/orders`, is the petstore's workflow table. Orders move through
`PLACED`, `APPROVED` and `DELIVERED`; each row offers only the transitions that are legal for its status, and
creating an order is a two-step dialog. It shows what row actions, dialogs, confirmations and a ribbon dialog button look
like when they are wired to real state changes.

## What this page shows

- **Server mode** with BeanQuery, like the Pets page, plus two URL-state directives, `day` and `window`. The query
  endpoint accepts `?day=yyyy-mm-dd`, or `?start=` and `?end=` for a date window (both ends inclusive, either may
  be omitted), and applies them before the column filters. A missing or malformed value is ignored. The Store page's
  trend chart links here with `?state=day({day})`.
- **Row actions with `visibleWhen`.** Approve appears only on `PLACED` rows and Deliver only on `APPROVED` rows.
  Each posts to `/console/orders/{id}/approve` or `/console/orders/{id}/deliver`; an illegal transition is a 409.
- **A dialog from an action.** Cancel opens a form (`GET /console/orders/{id}/cancel-form`, with a reason and a notify
  checkbox) and submits a `DELETE` to `/console/orders/{id}`. The reason is recorded in the audit trail.
- **A typed confirmation.** Delete uses `confirmRenderer: 'typed'`, so the user must type to confirm. The row
  action's `tone` is `danger`.
- **A two-step wizard.** The ribbon's "+ New order" button opens a `ModalDef`: step one picks an available pet and
  an optional ship date; its child action "Review order" stacks a second dialog, carrying the first step's inputs as
  drafts, and Confirm posts to `/console/orders`. Only pets that are for sale are offered.

description:
The Jobs page, served at `/console/ops/jobs`, is the petstore's reference for **asynchronous work**. A restock adds
new pets in the background: the browser submits it once, the server answers `202` with a job reference, and the page
follows the job's progress until it settles. The page also hosts a terminal demo, a "groom pet" job whose output is
streamed into a terminal card. If a write in your app takes longer than a request, copy this page.

## What this page shows

![The jobs page: restock form, job and species tables, and the grooming job streamed into terminal cards](/topics/PetstoreJobs.Page.1.png)

- **The mixin.** `JobsRest` implements `AsyncJobsMixin` and `TerminalMixin`. `AsyncJobsMixin` serves the stream and
  cancel operations under `/juneau-jobs`; the resource supplies the `AsyncJobRegistry` through `asyncJobRegistry()`.
- **Submit once.** `POST /console/ops/jobs/restock` builds an `IdempotencyKey` from the body's `idempotencyKey` and
  calls `AsyncJobRegistry.tryCreate(key)`. A resubmit with the same key returns the same job, so the resource keeps no
  key map of its own.
- **Self-targeted keys.** The ribbon "Restock" dialog has no row to bind a key to, so `restockForm()` returns a
  `ModalDef` carrying `IdempotencyKey.mintSelfTargeted("restock")` and the `selfTargeted` flag. The two must travel
  together; see [Rich Table Views: Actions](/docs/topics/RichTableViewsActions) for the pairing rule.
- **Completion.** The job finishes with a success `ActionResult` (`ActionResult.success(null)`, which
  `ActionResult.ok()` is the readability alias for) and a message such as "Restocked 3 pets".
- **A job-log card.** The "Restock inventory" card is a `job-log` card: a small submit form (counts per species, plus
  two timing knobs) that posts the same restock in its flat form, shows the job's progress lines and offers Cancel.
  `slowMs` waits before touching the store, so a cancel changes nothing; `holdMs` holds after the pets are added, so a
  late cancel ...

description:
The Audit page, served at `/console/ops/audit`, is the smallest server-mode table in the petstore and a leaf of the
navigation tree: one resource, one template, one query endpoint. It is a read-only view of the store's audit
trail, with a search box on every column and a date range on the timestamp. Start here if you want the shortest path
from a bean to a searchable table.

## What this page shows

- **A leaf page.** `AuditRest` has a page operation, a `POST /query` operation and a convenience `GET /rows`. It has no
  child resources and no write operations.
- **Server mode over BeanQuery.** `query` hands the DataTables request to `DataTablesQuery.run` against
  `store().queryAudit()`. A malformed search expression comes back as a 200 `error` envelope.
- **Typed column search.** Each column declares a `searchType`: `timestamp` for `at` and `text` for the rest. The
  `at` column takes a range as its search value, in the BeanQuery form
  `$between(2026-09-30T00:00:00Z,2026-10-01T00:00:00Z)`, and the query layer parses the ISO-8601 instants.
- **Newest first.** The default order is `at` descending. Mutations made through the console (for example a pet saved,
  an order approved or a restock job) write an `AuditEntry` with the actor, entity, entity id, action and detail.
- **Export.** Copy and CSV buttons in the ribbon.

## Template

The whole page is `audit.ftlh`, a single card:

```
<@card type="datatables" id="audit">{
  dataMode: 'server',
  dataUrl: '/console/ops/audit/query',
  defaultOrder: [{ key: 'at', dir: 'desc' }],
  columns: [
    { key: 'at', label: 'When', render: { id: 'timestamp' }, searchType: 'timestamp' },
    { key: 'actor', label: 'Actor', searchType: 'text' },
    { key: 'action', label: 'Action', searchType: 'text' }
  ],
  ribbon: [ { type: 'export', buttons: ['copy', 'csv'] }, { type: 'refresh', id: 'refresh' } ]
}</@card>
```

The excerpt trims three columns (`entity`, `entityId` and `detail`); the real card has six.

The Custom cards page (`/console/dev/cards`) shows how an adopter adds a card type of their own. It carries one
card type that needs no Java at all (`kpi`), one whose body the server validates and reshapes
(`inventory-gauge`), two ordinary `chart` cards fed by the same page, and two prose cards that exercise the card
API from a button row. Read it next to [Building a Console Page](/docs/topics/BuildingAConsolePage) when you
need a card the stock types do not cover.

## Two ways to write a card type

A card type is a JavaScript handler registered under a type id. A Java class is optional, and is worth adding only
when the server should validate or enrich the body before the page ships.

| Type | Java | Body | What the handler draws |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kpi` | none | `label` and `dataUrl` | One number from `/console/dev/cards/stats/available`, with its label |
| `inventory-gauge` | `InventoryGaugeCardType` | `species`, `low`, `high` | A gauge for one species, read from `/console/dev/cards/inventory?species=` |

Both handlers live in the page script `petstore-cards.js`, served beside `CustomCardsRest`. The page loads it
through `init`, and the handlers register by pushing onto `window.JuneauConsoleCards`. That queue works whether
your script runs before or after the console shell:

```js
(window.JuneauConsoleCards = window.JuneauConsoleCards || []).push(['kpi', {
  render(card, el, ctx) { ... }
}]);
```

With no registered Java handler, a type falls back to the generic passthrough: the JSON5 body becomes the card
fragment unchanged. That is all `kpi` is.

`InventoryGaugeCardType` implements `CardTypeHandler`. Its `toFragment` rejects a body with no `species`, an
unknown species, a non-whole `low` or `high`, a negative `low`, or `low` at or above `high`. `low` defaults to 0
and `high` to 100. A good body is reshaped into a `gauge` object that adds the `dataUrl` for that species, which is
what the browser handler draws. A bad body fails the pa...

description:
The Pending changes page (`/console/pets/changes`) lists edits that were staged from the pet detail page but not yet
written to the pet. A staged change can be applied, retried if the write failed, or discarded. The same page is the
data source for the count badge in the console header, which is why this page is also where the `<@badge>`
directive is documented: the framework has no page of its own for it yet.

## The PendingChange lifecycle

`PendingChanges` (obtained from `PetStore.pendingChanges()`) holds the staged edits, and a `PendingChange` has one
of three states:

| State | Meaning | Allowed next step |
|---|---|---|
| `PENDING` | Staged. The pet is unchanged. | Apply, or discard |
| `APPLIED` | Written to the pet, and the write is audited. | None |
| `FAILED` | The apply failed, for example because the pet is gone. `message` says why. | Retry |

Staging records the field, the old value, the new value, the author and a one-line `summary` in the form
`<pet name>: <field> '<old>' -> '<new>'`. The staging call is `POST /console/pets/{id}/stage`, served by `PetsRest`.

:::note The photo is not stageable
Every editable Pet field stages into a pending change except the photo. The photo is a binary payload with no
meaningful diff and nothing sensible to discard, so staging it is rejected with a 400,
`Field 'photo' cannot be staged; use one of: name, price, species, status, tags`. The pet detail Photo tab edits it
directly. See [Petstore: Pet Detail](/docs/topics/PetstorePetDetail).
:::

## Apply, retry and discard

| Route | Does | Errors |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /console/pets/changes/{id}/apply` | Writes one `PENDING` change to its pet | 404 unknown change, 409 not pending |
| `POST /console/pets/changes/{id}/retry` | Re-applies one `FAILED` change | 404 unknown change, 409 not failed |
| `POST /console/pets/changes/discard` | Discards many `PENDING` changes in one call | 400 missing `ids` or `idempotencyKey` |

description:
The Users page (`/console/users`) is the petstore's server-mode CRUD example: a table of user accounts with a status
filter, an add dialog in the ribbon, and Edit and Delete row actions. Its one lesson beyond the plain table is the
password. It is write-only: it can be set from the form, but nothing the server sends ever contains it.

## The table

The table pages, sorts and filters on the server. `UsersRest.query` runs the DataTables request through
`DataTablesQuery.run` and answers a malformed search expression with a 200 `error` envelope, as the other
server-mode pages do. The ribbon has a deselectable "User status" option group (`$eq(ACTIVE)` and `$eq(INACTIVE)`
on the `userStatus` column), the "+ Add user" dialog button and a refresh button. The row actions are Edit, which
opens the same form in a dialog, and Delete, which confirms first and is styled as dangerous.

## The write-only password

Every read goes through a `UserView` record that has username, first name, last name and status, and no password
field. The query runs over `UserView` through its own `InMemoryBeanQueryContext`, so the password is neither
searchable nor serialized. `GET /console/users/{username}` returns the same view. The result toast of a create or an
update carries a `UserView` too.

The dialog is built by `GET /console/users/form` as a `ModalDef` with a `FormDef`:

| Case | Password field |
|---|---|
| Add (no `username` query parameter) | Required, with the help text "Write-only; it is never shown again" |
| Edit (`?username=`) | Optional, never pre-filled, with the help text "Leave blank to keep the current password" |

The field is a masked `password` input and never carries a `value`. On update, a field left out of the body keeps
its stored value, and a null or blank password keeps the stored password. Both the plain body and the dialog
envelope (`{fields: {...}}`) are accepted.

| Route | Does | Errors |
|---|---|---|
| `POST /console/users/query` | One page of `UserView` rows...

The Rendering flavors section (`/console/dev/flavors`) shows the same list of ten pets drawn by four different view
technologies, each inside the console chrome: the HTML5 bean builder, FreeMarker, Mustache and the standalone React
app. It replaces the earlier standalone view resources with pages inside the console. Each flavor is a level-3
subtab under Developer, so a reader can flip between them and compare the output.

## Four subtabs

`FlavorsRest` (`/console/dev/flavors`) redirects `/` to the first flavor with a 303 to `html`. The enum `Flavor`
holds each flavor's id, nav label, caption and the GitHub link to its source. The nav tree in `base.ftlh` lists them
as the nodes `html`, `freemarker`, `mustache` and `react` under `flavors`.

| Subtab | Resource | What serves the list |
|---|---|---|
| `html` | `HtmlFlavorRest` | A `Table` built with the HTML5 bean builder, serialized by `HtmlSerializer` |
| `freemarker` | `FreemarkerFlavorRest` | The `fragments/pets.ftlh` template through the FreeMarker view bridge |
| `mustache` | `MustacheFlavorRest` | A `pets.mustache` template through `MustacheViewRenderer` and a `MustacheMixin` |
| `react` | `FlavorsRest.react` | The standalone app at `/petstore-ui`, embedded in an iframe |

All three server flavors draw the same rows. `FlavorPets.rows` returns the first ten pets by id with display-ready
strings (the price has two decimals), so the engines differ only in markup.

## Chrome-less fragments

Each server flavor is a child resource that serves two things: its console page at `/`, and a bare fragment at
`/fragment` with no page chrome. The console page is one `html` card whose content comes from the fragment through
`src=`. The fragment is a `<table class="petstore-flavor" data-flavor="...">`, so a test can tell the engines apart
and compare their cells exactly. The FreeMarker fragment carries no `<@page>` for the same reason: it is loaded into
a card, not served as a page.

description:
The Secure page (`/console/dev/secure`) pairs an open console page with a bearer-token protected API underneath it.
Its "Try it" card calls the API from your browser with no token, with a demo token and with a wrong token, and prints
the status and body, so you see the 401 and the success side by side. The page also marks the line between two
different protections: the bearer guard on the API, and the CSRF boundary that guards writes to the console itself.
This page covers both, adds the separate CSRF boundary on the `/petstore` API, and shows how the Jetty and Spring Boot
runners install the boundaries.

## The bearer-token demo

The page is open. The API under `/console/dev/secure/api` is `SecureApiRest`, and every operation on it is gated by
a fail-closed `BearerTokenGuard` with the realm `petstore`, backed by `StubBearerTokenValidator`:

| Request | Result |
|---|---|
| No `Authorization` header | 401, with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="petstore"` |
| `Authorization: Bearer petstore-user` | 200, principal `alice` |
| `Authorization: Bearer petstore-admin` | 200, principal `admin` |
| Any other token | 401 |

The API has `GET /pets`, `GET /pets/{id}` (404 for an unknown pet) and `GET /whoami`, which returns the caller's
name through an `@Auth Principal` parameter. The guard is one `@Bean` returning a `RestGuardList`, so it covers every
operation on the resource. The siblings stay open: the guard does not touch `/petstore` or the other console pages.
From a shell:

```
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer petstore-user' http://localhost:10000/console/dev/secure/api/pets
```

With a single mechanism, the op-level guard is the whole story. `AuthFilterChain` is for composing several
mechanisms; it is fail-open by design, so a downstream guard still decides.

## The CSRF boundary

Everything under `/console` is also behind `PetstoreConsoleBoundary`, a servlet `Filter` over the framework's
`LoopbackBoundaryFilter`. It pins the `Host` header on every console request, an...

the pet store itself. Three of them are about charts and data: Charts, Data sources and Dashboard. All three are
builder-only pages. Each is written as a `PageSpec` in Java and has no FreeMarker twin and no navigation node of its

[Custom Cards](/docs/topics/PetstoreCustomCards), [Themes](/docs/topics/PetstoreThemes),

description:
Every page in the petstore console is written twice. One copy is a FreeMarker template (`.ftlh`) that uses the
console directives. The other is a Java method that builds the same page with `PageSpec` and `TableSpec`. The two are
called twins, and a test proves they stay the same page. This page explains why the petstore keeps both, shows one
pair side by side, and ends with a recipe for your own console.

## Why twins exist

The console renders a page from a *page contract*: a JSON document in `#juneau-page` plus one `<template>` per card.
A template and a builder are two ways to produce that same contract.

- A **template** reads like the page. The card body is JSON5, so what you write is what the browser gets. It is the
  right default for a page whose shape you know when you write it.
- A **builder** composes the page in Java. It can loop, call helpers, share a table definition between two pages, and
  check column names against a bean at compile time. It is the right tool when the page is computed.

The petstore writes both for every page so that each form has a worked, tested example, and so the tests can prove
the builder covers everything a template can say. Each page on the tour has a "Builder twin" section with its own
pair.

The template is what a normal request serves. Adding `?builder` to the URL renders the builder twin instead, and the
response carries the header `X-Petstore-Page: builder` so a test can tell the two paths apart. `?mixed` renders a
third form, covered below.

description:
A console page that is misconfigured must fail where the mistake is, with a message that names it. It must not render
a half-working page, drop a card, or fall back to a default without telling anyone. The petstore calls this
*FailLoud*. This page explains the rule, shows how the tests exercise it, and lists every case the petstore pins.

## What FailLoud means

When a template or a `PageSpec` is wrong, the render stops with HTTP 500 and the body names the directive, the id and
what to do instead. For example, a badge declared twice, a nav path that does not exist, a body key that is
reserved, or a `bytesUrl` that points off-site. The message is the contract. The tests assert the text of the
message, not just the status, so a rewording that loses the useful part fails the build.

Two things are worth knowing before you read the table:

- **Most cases pin a message, not a code.** The reason codes the console used to print (the `E-B` series for the
  server-side directives) were replaced by plain messages, so the table lists a code only where an assertion still
  pins one. A code that appears only in a comment does not count.
- **Some failures are client-side.** The server renders the page successfully and the browser script reports the
  problem. Those are covered separately, below the main table.

## How the tests are built

`PetstoreFailLoud_Test` renders small fixture templates through three hosts. Each is a minimal REST servlet with the
console FreeMarker mixin:

- `FixtureHost` renders `failloud/<name>.ftlh` inside the production `base.ftlh` chrome, so a fixture is a page in the
  real petstore frame. It also has two builder routes (`/s/badge-duplicate` and `/s/facts-duplicate`) for mistakes
  that start in a `PageSpec`, and it registers the petstore's custom card type so the custom-card cases run for real.
- `DevHost` is the same chrome with dev mode on. Dev mode validates each page contract against its schema before
  writing it, so a bad contract is reject...

description:
The petstore console is a worked example. This page is the short version of "how do I bring these patterns into an
admin UI I already have": which of the four patterns to take, what each one needs from your app, and how to choose
which to adopt. It does not repeat the framework pages. Each
section points at the page that owns the detail and at the petstore page that shows it running.

Start with the [tour overview](/docs/topics/JuneauPetstore) and the [Console Tour](/docs/topics/PetstoreConsoleTour)
if you have not seen the console yet. If you are building a page from scratch rather than porting, read
[Building a Console Page](/docs/topics/BuildingAConsolePage) instead.

## Before you port anything

Move the chrome first. The four patterns below all assume the console shell is in place: a `<@console>` base template,
a `<@navigation>` tree and the shared assets from `ConsoleChromeMixin`. Without it there is no header to hang a badge
on and no card runtime to mount a job log. The chrome is described in
[Admin-Console Chrome](/docs/topics/AdminConsoleChrome), and the petstore's version of it is on
[Console Tour](/docs/topics/PetstoreConsoleTour).

Then take the patterns one at a time. They are independent, so you can adopt any subset. A good order, from least to
most design work:

1. the async-job plumbing (mostly a swap of what you already have);
2. the audit page (a read-only view);
3. the header badge (one endpoint and one directive);
4. staged edits (the one that changes how your app behaves).

## Header badge

A badge is a small counter in the page header that polls a JSON endpoint and links to the page that explains the
number. The petstore uses it for the count of pending changes.

What you need:

- a count endpoint that answers `GET` with a JSON object carrying a numeric `total`;
- one `<@badge>` directive in the base template, placed **after** `</@navigation>`, not inside the navigation block.

Leave the badge unscoped unless you want it hidden on other sec...

description:
Apache Juneau ships two packaging aids that make it easy to depend on a coherent, version-aligned slice
of the framework without hand-maintaining a long list of `<version>` tags:

- A **Bill of Materials (BOM)** — `org.apache.juneau:juneau-bom` — for version alignment.
- A small set of curated **dependency bundles** — one per deployment shape — that transitively pull a
  coherent module set.

Both are deliberately **dependency-only** aids. They register nothing and discover nothing at runtime
(see [Explicit over magic](#explicit-over-magic-no-auto-configuration) below).

## The BOM

The `${juneau.version}` property is `10.0.0-SNAPSHOT` for these docs; the latest release on Maven Central is 9.2.0. See [Install Juneau](/docs/topics/GettingStartedInstall#set-the-version).

The BOM is a 10.0 artifact; it is not published for 9.2.0.

Import `juneau-bom` (scope `import`, type `pom`) in your `<dependencyManagement>` and then drop the
explicit versions from every Juneau dependency — the BOM supplies them:

```xml
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId>
            <artifactId>juneau-bom</artifactId>
            <version>${juneau.version}</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
    <!-- No <version> needed - the BOM aligns it. -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId>
        <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId>
        <artifactId>juneau-rest-server</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

The BOM enumerates the **consumer-facing** Juneau modules (juneau-core marshalling/config, juneau-rest,
juneau-microservice, juneau-bean, juneau-sc), the test-support modules (`juneau-bct`,
`juneau-microservice-test`, `juneau-rest-mock`), and the curated `*-bundle` POMs themselves. It ...

description:
This page covers two packaging concerns for Juneau applications: **Docker image layering** (a concrete recommendation you can apply today) and **GraalVM native-image** support (a feasibility assessment with a forward plan).

## Docker image layering

Juneau itself ships **libraries**, not runnable applications, so there is no Juneau-side fat-jar to layer. Layering happens in *your* deployable application image. Two practical levers:

- **Spring Boot apps** — `spring-boot-maven-plugin`'s `repackage` goal produces a [layered jar](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/packaging/efficient.html) by default (since Spring Boot 2.4), separating slow-changing dependency layers from your fast-changing application classes. Combined with a multi-stage Dockerfile using `java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers`, Docker caches the dependency layer across rebuilds. The Juneau Spring Boot petstore sample is built this way.
- **Embedded-Jetty / plain-jar apps** — order your Dockerfile `COPY` steps coarsest-changing first: copy the dependency jars (which include the stable Juneau artifacts) in an earlier layer than your application jar, so a code-only change re-uploads only the small application layer. The [starter projects](/docs/topics/StarterProjects) on the `apache/juneau` `microservice-*-starter` branches ship minimal Dockerfiles; a production image can apply the layered `COPY` shape described above.

Depending on Juneau through the version-aligned [BOM and curated bundles](/docs/topics/DependencyManagement) keeps the dependency layer stable and reproducible across rebuilds, which is what makes the cache hit reliable.

## GraalVM native-image — feasibility verdict

Juneau's marshalling/bean core is reflection-heavy, so native-image (closed-world AOT) support is non-trivial. A feasibility assessment was performed against the reflective source; the verdict is **CONDITIONAL GO**.

### Why "conditional go", not "no-go"

`juneau-terminal` is build tooling, not a library dependency. It ships `juneau_terminal.py`, a stdlib-only Python script that
wraps Maven, pytest, Playwright, Gradle, npm and Bazel runs. It parses each tool's output into steps, sub-steps and
test counts, and from those it draws a board console view, writes full and board logs, prints terminal-protocol
markers for a runner UI, and writes terminal-view events for the [Terminal View Region](/docs/topics/TerminalViewRegion) and the
[Terminal Region](/docs/topics/TerminalRegion). Juneau's own `test.py`, `push.py` and `release.py` run on it.

The module is `pom` packaging and attaches its files to `org.apache.juneau:juneau-terminal:<version>`:

| Type | Classifier | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| `py` | | `juneau_terminal.py`, the engine. |
| `zip` | | `bootstrap.py`, the `juneau_terminal_scripts` toolkit for push and release scripts, the pytest plugin and the Playwright reporter. |
| `py` | `pytest` | The pytest plugin on its own. |

It is not managed by `juneau-bom`; pin it at the Juneau version your build already uses. `mvn install` in the module
runs its unit tests (`python3 -m unittest`); `-DskipTests` skips them. PTY mode is POSIX only.

:::note
Using the Maven artifact, or a vendored copy, and running `mvn install` in the module, is the interim way to get
`juneau-terminal` until Juneau 10.0.0 is released. For the 10.0 release the plan is to publish it as a PyPI package,
`apache-juneau-terminal` (installed with `uv tool install` or `pipx`), as a runnable `.pyz`, and as a Homebrew tap
(`brew install apache/juneau/juneau-terminal`, the CLI only). The Playwright reporter is planned for npm as
`@apache/juneau-terminal-playwright`. These are plans, and the details may change.

description:
An AI coding agent such as Claude Code runs a shell command and shows its output when the command finishes. A
six-minute `push.py` or Maven gate is therefore a silent wait: no progress, no sign of which module is building. This
page shows how to give the run a live pane beside the chat, using tmux and [juneau-terminal](/docs/topics/JuneauTerminal)'s
board view.

## The approach

1. Run the agent inside tmux.
2. Have the agent start the long command in a side pane. The pane has a real terminal, so juneau-terminal draws its live
   view there, and focus stays where you are typing. This is the **leader** pane.
3. A second pane, the **follower**, sits below it. It runs `tail -F` on the full log, so you also see every line of
   output, not only the board rows.
4. The agent blocks until the command is done.
5. It reads the result back from the pane's last lines and the command's exit code, and carries on.

You watch the run as it happens. The agent still gets what it needs: the final rows and a pass or fail.

![An agent pane beside a leader pane and a follower pane](/topics/AgentSidePane.Approach.1.svg)

## What juneau-terminal contributes

With `JUNEAU_TERMINAL_CONSOLE=board` (or `--console board`), a run in the leader pane shows:

- one row per step, with its time, a progress bar, counts and a line of summary;
- the module bar for a Maven build, and a dot line under each running module, test file or check;
- a header that prints the `tail -f` command for the full log.

By default the full log is written under `~/.cache/juneau-terminal/` (the newest 20 are kept), so the agent can read the
details of a failure without scrolling the pane. A run also accepts the paths up front, in `JUNEAU_TERMINAL_FULL_LOG` and
`JUNEAU_TERMINAL_BOARD_LOG`; `watch-run.sh` uses that. See [Console view](/docs/topics/JuneauTerminal#console-view) for the
options.

## The scripts

The toolkit zip, `org.apache.juneau:juneau-terminal:<version>:zip`, carries two bash scripts in `juneau_terminal_...

description:
A script built on [juneau-terminal](/docs/topics/JuneauTerminal) draws its live view for whoever is watching the terminal. A tool
that starts the script (an AI coding agent, an IDE task, a CI wrapper) needs something else: progress it can follow
and an outcome it can read, without scraping a screen. This page shows how to give each of them what they need from
the same run.

## The pattern

1. The person gets a real terminal that shows the live view: a tmux pane, an IDE console or a CI log.
2. The tool follows the run's progress in the **markers file**, `JUNEAU_TERMINAL_MARKERS_FILE`.
3. When the run ends, the tool reads the **result file**, `JUNEAU_TERMINAL_RESULT`: the status, the exit code and one row
   per step.
4. Anyone else who wants the details reads the logs. The result file names the full log and the board log.

Neither file changes what the terminal shows. With `TERMINAL_MARKERS` unset, the run draws its console view as usual, and
the markers go to the file as well.

![An agent pane beside a run pane](/topics/AgentSidePane.Approach.1.svg)

## The two files

Both are written by the script that owns the run, the one that calls `run()` and `done()` (Juneau's own `push.py` and
`test.py` are such scripts).

`JUNEAU_TERMINAL_MARKERS_FILE=<path>`
: Every [terminal-protocol](https://github.com/apache/juneau/blob/master/juneau-terminal/docs/terminal-protocol-v1.md) marker, one
  `##terminal {json}` line each. The owner empties the file when the run starts. A script it runs, which inherits
  `JUNEAU_TERMINAL_ACTIVE`, appends its steps to the same file. A file that can't be written is reported once on stderr and
  the run goes on without it. Under `--pty` the file isn't written.

`JUNEAU_TERMINAL_RESULT=<path>`
: One JSON object, written when the run ends (ok, failed, or cancelled by Ctrl-C or SIGTERM). It is written through
  a temporary file and a rename, so a reader never sees half of it, and an older file at that path is removed when the
  run starts. Fields ...

description:
Juneau provides **shaded (uber) JAR artifacts** that bundle multiple Juneau modules into single JAR files. These artifacts simplify dependency management and are especially useful for build systems like Bazel that require explicit dependency declarations.

## What Are Shaded Artifacts?

Shaded artifacts use the [Maven Shade Plugin](https://maven.apache.org/plugins/maven-shade-plugin/) to:
- Bundle multiple Juneau modules into a single JAR
- Merge service provider files automatically
- Eliminate the need to declare transitive Juneau dependencies
- Maintain all original functionality without modification

**Important**: Shaded artifacts only bundle Juneau modules. External dependencies (like Apache HttpClient, Jakarta Servlet API, etc.) must still be declared separately.

## Available Shaded Artifacts

|----------|------|-------------|---------|
| [juneau-shaded-core](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedCore) | 2.0 MB | Core marshalling and configuration functionality | [Learn more →](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedCore) |
| [juneau-shaded-rest-client](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedRestClient) | 3.8 MB | Core + REST client functionality | [Learn more →](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedRestClient) |
| [juneau-shaded-rest-server](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedRestServer) | 3.8 MB | Core + REST server functionality | [Learn more →](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedRestServer) |
| [juneau-shaded-rest-server-springboot](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedRestServerSpringboot) | 3.8 MB | REST server + Spring Boot integration | [Learn more →](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedRestServerSpringboot) |
| [juneau-shaded-all](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedAll) | 4.0 MB | Complete Juneau framework in one JAR | [Learn more →](/docs/topics/JuneauShadedAll) |

## When to Use Shaded Artifacts

### ✅ Use Shaded Artifacts When:

- **Using Bazel or similar build systems** - These require explicit dependency declarations; shaded artifacts simplify this significantly
- **Wanting simplified dependency managem...

This artifact includes the following Juneau modules:

- **juneau-commons** - Core utilities and common classes

- **SOAP/XML** - SOAP-style XML

- **Serialization/Deserialization** - Convert POJOs to/from various formats
- **Configuration Management** - Use the Config API for application settings

description:
Apache Juneau provides three minimal, clone-and-go **"Hello World" starter projects** — one per
deployment type. They are deliberately simpler than the [petstore showcase](/docs/topics/JuneauPetstore):
entry-point templates you can build and run in under five minutes, then graduate from.

:::note Pre-release
Juneau 10 is a pre-release (`10.0.0-SNAPSHOT`). Each starter's `pom.xml` already points at the Apache snapshots
repository, so a normal Maven build resolves it with no extra setup, but it needs network access and the
snapshot can change between builds. Maven Central has only 9.2.0 today (see [Downloads](/downloads)), and the
starters need 10.0, so they cannot build without that repository. See
[Set the version](/docs/topics/GettingStartedInstall#set-the-version).
:::

New to Juneau? The [Getting Started](/docs/topics/GettingStarted) walkthrough builds a small REST app from an
empty directory and does not need a starter.

Each starter is a **true-orphan branch** of [`apache/juneau`](https://github.com/apache/juneau).
Clone one branch into a `my-app` directory (single-branch; not a full Java checkout):

```bash
git clone -b microservice-jetty-starter --single-branch https://github.com/apache/juneau.git my-app
git clone -b microservice-springboot-starter --single-branch https://github.com/apache/juneau.git my-app
git clone -b microservice-tomcat-starter --single-branch https://github.com/apache/juneau.git my-app
```

| Starter | Deployment | Branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jetty | Embedded Jetty, runnable jar | `microservice-jetty-starter` |
| Spring Boot | Spring Boot, runnable jar | `microservice-springboot-starter` |
| Tomcat | WAR on Tomcat 10.1+ | `microservice-tomcat-starter` |

Each starter demonstrates a lean, Juneau-native feature set: a POJO-returning resource (JSON/XML/HTML
content negotiation), the built-in HtmlDoc view, an auto-generated Swagger/OPTIONS page, `@Path`/`@Query`
binding, a YAML config file, and a `MockRestClient` example test exercising...
summary: Apache Juneau provides three minimal, clone-and-go **"Hello World" starter projects** — one per deployment type. They are deliberately simpler than the [petstore showcase](/docs/topics/JuneauPetstore): entry-point templates you can build and run in under five minutes, then graduate from.
title: Starter Projects

description: Security is an ongoing concern in any library. Juneau is designed so that its serializers and parsers are safe by default — POJO types are inferred from the `Class` objects you pass in rather than from attacker-controlled input — but a few areas warrant care when you extend the framework or expose it over HTTP. This section covers the security characteristics of each layer: - **[Marshalling Security](/docs/topics/MarshallingSecurity)** — why the parsers are not subject to arbitrary-object (demarshalling) attacks, how bean dictionaries replace open-ended `class` attributes, and the security posture of the dependent parsing libraries. - **[SVL Security](/docs/topics/SvlSecurity)** — how the Simple Variable Language guards against variable-injection and file-disclosure attacks via the `Var.allowNested()` / `Var.allowRecurse()` controls, and what to watch for when writing your own variables. - **[REST Security](/docs/topics/RestSecurity)** — mitigating denial-of-service attacks through the `maxInput()` setting and the parsers' streaming (non-DOM) design. - **[Content Security Policy](/docs/topics/ContentSecurityPolicy)** — locking down Juneau's auto-generated HTML pages (HtmlDoc, Swagger UI, OpenAPI UI, widgets) with a first-class Content-Security-Policy header bean. If you discover a security vulnerability in Juneau, please follow the responsible-disclosure instructions in [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/apache/juneau/blob/master/SECURITY.md) rather than opening a public issue. ## In This Section

description:
## Demarshalling vulnerabilities

One common security vulnerability is the ability to create arbitrary Java object instances through crafted user input.

For example, support for constructing POJOs based on an input attribute defining a fully-qualified class name like
`{class:'com.foo.MyBean',...}`

Fortunately, Juneau does not support an open-ended `class` attribute.

As a rule, it should not be possible to create arbitrary POJOs by any of the parsers.

The demarshalled object types are inferred via reflection of the class objects passed in through the parser method (e.g.
`JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(input, MyBean.class)`).

As long as the `Class` object passed into this method is not constructed from user-generated input, it should be free
from demarshalling vulnerabilities.

The following example shows a potential vector that circumvents the restriction above:

```java
// Don't do this!
Class c = Class.forName(someUserInputString);
JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(input, c);  // Oops!  Security hole!
```

Juneau does support something similar to a `class` attribute that allows you to define the POJO type at runtime.
This is the `type` attribute.
The difference is that it's not possible to specify fully-qualified class names in `type` attributes, and instead can
only specify type keys defined through bean dictionaries.
Instead of serializing the fully-qualified class names in the output, we instead serialize type names that represent
those POJO types.
i.e.
instead of `class='com.foo.MyBean'`, we instead serialize `type='MyBeanIdentifier'`.
Since bean types are defined at compile time, it's impossible to instantiate arbitrary POJOs.
POJO types of generalized input are also inferred through swaps.
Again, since the POJO types are hardcoded at compile time, these should not be subject to demarshalling vulnerabilities.
However, it is possible to circumvent this through your swap implementation as shown below:

public class MyInsecureSwap extends ObjectS...

description: Care must be used when defining new Vars using the SVL API since mistakes could potentially expose system properties, environment variables, or even file system files. For recap, the SVL support allows you to embed variables of the form `$X{key}` inside strings that get resolved to other strings. The resolved strings themselves can also contain variables that also get recursively resolved. An example of a potential security hole is shown below that could potentially expose any file on a file system through a REST request: ```java public String doUnsafeGet(RestRequest req) { // Security hole! return req.getVarResolver().resolve("$RQ{foo}"); } ``` This code is simply echoing the value of the `foo` query parameter. Now say for example that a bad actor passes in the query string `foo=$F{/some/file/on/file/system}`. The `$F` variable allows you to resolve the contents of files using SVL, and is provided by default using the built-in variable resolver returned by the `RestRequest` object. You've potentially just exposed the contents of that file through your REST interface. In reality, the above security hole does not exist because of the following restrictions: - `Vars` have two methods Var.allowNested() and Var.allowRecurse() that can be overridden to prevent recursive processing of string variables. These both return `false` for the `$RQ` request-query variable, so the `$F` variable embedded in the result will never get processed and is instead treated as plain text. - The `$F` variable does not read arbitrary files off the filesystem. It resolves contents through the REST context's configured static-files resolver (`RestContext.getStaticFiles()`), so it can only retu...

description: Denial of service attacks can be alleviated through the maxInput() setting. Arbitrarily-large input will trigger an exception before causing out-of-memory errors. The default value for this setting is 100MB. Since the parsers do not use intermediate DOMs and instead parse directly into Java objects, deeply nested data structures will almost always trigger stack overflow errors long before memory consumption becomes an issue. However, this is NOT true of the RDF parsers, which build an intermediate DOM. If parsing RDF, you may want to consider lowering the max-input value above. ## CSRF protection: loopback vs general Juneau ships two request boundaries in `org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter`. Both decide whether a state-changing request came from a page your application served (or from a non-browser client) and refuse it when it came from some other site's page. Neither one authenticates the caller, and neither proves the user meant the action; those need their own mechanisms. | Boundary | Use it when | |---|---| | `LoopbackBoundary` | The app is bound to the loopback interface and is reached under one pinned `Host` (for example `127.0.0.1:8790`) over plain HTTP. It pins that single origin and is the stricter of the two. | | `CsrfBoundary` | Everything else: an app reached under a real host name, over HTTPS, behind a proxy, or under more than one name. Nothing is pinned; the request's own scheme and host are the expected origin. | Both are applied by `RequestBoundaryFilter`. A rejected request is answered directly with a JSON body, a `Cache-Control: no-store` header, and an `X-Request-Boundary` header naming the reason (for example `ORIGIN_MISMATCH` or `CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING`). The request never reaches application code. Even without a boundary, the router refuses an override of a safe method (`GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `TRACE`) to an unsafe one with `405`. A bo...

description:
The following guide can be used to help migrate your code to v10.0.
Note that you can also refer to the Release Notes for changes as well.

This guide covers all breaking changes introduced since v9.1, including changes that were
originally developed under the v9.5.0 label (a release that was never shipped — it was
renamed to v10.0.0). Teams upgrading from 8.x, 9.1, or any earlier version can use this
as a single authoritative reference.

## Package Renames

### REST Server Package Rename: `org.apache.juneau.rest.*` → `org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*`

All server-side REST classes have been moved from `org.apache.juneau.rest` to `org.apache.juneau.rest.server`.
This affects the core module as well as all server add-on modules (`-auth-jwt`, `-mcp`, `-metrics-micrometer`,
`-auth-oauth`, `-auth-oidc-rp`, `-tracing-otel`, `-rdf`, `-reactive`, `-reactive-reactor`, `-auth-saml`,
`-springboot`, `-view-*`). Client-side classes (`org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*`) and mock testing classes
(`org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.*`) are **not affected**. Additionally, the `juneau-rest-server-reactive-reactor`
module had its package renamed from `org.apache.juneau.rest.server.reactor` →
`org.apache.juneau.rest.server.reactive.reactor` to match the new module name.

**Migration:** Update all `import org.apache.juneau.rest.X` → `import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.X` in user
code. IDE global find-replace on the import prefix is sufficient.

### Marshall Package Rename: `org.apache.juneau.*` (marshall classes) → `org.apache.juneau.marshall.*`

All classes from the `juneau-marshall` and `juneau-marshall-rdf` modules have been moved from the root
`org.apache.juneau` namespace into the `org.apache.juneau.marshall` namespace. This includes all
format-specific subpackages (`json`, `xml`, `html`, `yaml`, `csv`, `uon`, `urlencoding`, `msgpack`, `cbor`,
`bson`, `json5`, `jsonl`, `jsonschema`, `markdown`, `plaintext`, `oapi`, `proto`, `soap`, `sse`, `parquet`,
`toml`, `hocon`, `hjson`, `ini`, `j...
